title: The employment measurement dispute
summary: The official Periodic Labour Force Survey and the private CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey disagree on the direction of employment change, not merely its magnitude. PLFS shows unemployment falling 6.0% to 3.2% with participation rising sharply; CMIE shows unemployment at 7-9% throughout and, over 2017-18 to 2021-22, employment growth of the opposite sign.
whatHappened: The first PLFS round was withheld past its December 2018 release date. In January 2019 the acting chairman of the National Statistical Commission, P.C. Mohanan, and member J.V. Meenakshi resigned in protest. The report was leaked showing 6.1% unemployment, a 45-year high, and was dismissed by ministers as a draft — Mohanan's response was that having approved it, it was not a draft. It was released officially on 31 May 2019, days after the election, confirming the figure. The divergence with CMIE persists and is concentrated almost entirely among women, whose measured participation in official data runs roughly double CMIE's with no convergence across reference periods.
caseFor: PLFS is the statutory national survey: large sample, Census-consistent demographics, ILO-standard definitions, and public unit-level microdata that anyone can re-analyse. CMIE is private, subscription-gated, and its sampling frame has been criticised by serious economists including a former Chief Economic Adviser. The 2019 delay was procedurally poor but the report was published unaltered, and a government suppressing data would not release the number that embarrassed it.
caseAgainst: A national survey whose headline rate falls because unpaid family work is counted as employment cannot be cited as evidence that jobs were created, whatever its sampling quality. The withholding of the first round until after a general election, and two statistical commissioners resigning over it, is a governance fact independent of the survey's technical merits. And a private survey being inconvenient is not a methodological argument against it.
shockExposure: Demonetisation (November 2016) and GST (July 2017) both fall inside the first PLFS reference year, so the 6.1% baseline itself sits on disturbed ground. COVID then dominates every 2019-2022 comparison.
caveat: This record must not be resolved in either direction. The instruments answer different questions: PLFS supports statements about participation and status composition, CMIE about open joblessness among urban, educated and female workers. Any view presenting one as the employment picture is misrepresenting the evidence.

sources.name: Resignation of NSC members over the withheld PLFS report

title: The falling unemployment rate and what produced it
summary: PLFS unemployment fell from 6.0% (2017-18) to 3.2% (2023-24) while participation rose from 49.8% to 60.1%. Decomposed, the improvement is predominantly absorption into self-employment, unpaid family labour and agriculture rather than firm-led hiring.
whatHappened: The self-employed share of workers rose to 58.4% and the unpaid-helper share from 13.3% to 17.3%, while regular wage and salaried employment stayed flat at 21-23%. Agriculture's employment share, which had fallen for decades to 42.5% in 2018-19, rose to 46.1% by 2023-24; in 2019-20 alone agricultural employment rose by about 32 million, absorbing roughly three-quarters of that year's total employment increase. Manufacturing's employment share fell from 12.1% to 11.4%.
caseFor: Participation rising by ten percentage points while unemployment fell is not nothing — more people were working, and in a labour surplus economy absorbing them at all is an achievement. Self-employment is how most of the developing world works and treating it as failure imports an assumption about what a job should look like. Agriculture's rise is substantially a COVID artefact, with workers returning to villages when urban work collapsed, and it has begun to moderate.
caseAgainst: Every quality indicator moved the wrong way while the headline improved. Regular wage employment, the only category that reliably carries contracts, leave and social security, did not grow at all. Real rural earnings fell from ₹9,107 to ₹8,842 a month. And agriculture's share rising is a reversal of structural transformation — the process by which countries get richer — so the same data read as a development indicator says the economy moved backwards.
shockExposure: COVID dominates: the 2020-21 and 2021-22 readings are shaped by lockdown, reverse migration and agricultural absorption. But the agricultural share had already turned upward in 2019-20, before the pandemic.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (phase 15 batch 13); this record carried a `contested` verdict with no stated ground. THE TWO READINGS USE THE SAME SERIES AND DIFFER ON WHAT COUNTS AS IMPROVEMENT. Agreed on both sides: participation rose about ten percentage points, measured unemployment fell, regular wage employment did not grow, real rural earnings fell from Rs 9,107 to Rs 8,842 a month, and agriculture's share of employment rose. Reading one is ABSORPTION: in a labour-surplus economy, drawing ten points more of the population into work at all is an achievement, self-employment is how most of the developing world works, and the agricultural rise is substantially a COVID artefact already moderating. Reading two is STRUCTURAL TRANSFORMATION: every quality indicator moved the wrong way, and a rising agricultural share is the reversal of the process by which countries get richer — so the same data read as a development indicator says the economy went backwards. THE RECORD DECLINES BECAUSE THE DISAGREEMENT IS NORMATIVE. The dispute is over the criterion, not the measurement, and the instrument's rule against composite scores forbids resolving it by weighting quantity against quality. NOT a case of work left undone.
revisitTrigger: A regular-wage-employment series extending past the current window, or a real-earnings series by employment category, would sharpen reading two; neither settles the criterion question.

title: Female labour force participation reversal
summary: Female labour force participation rose from 23.3% (2017-18) to 41.7% (2023-24) — among the largest increases recorded anywhere — reversing a long decline that had taken rural female participation from 49.4% in 2004-05 to 35.8% in 2011-12. THE TWO HALVES OF THAT SENTENCE ARE NOT ONE SERIES. The 2004-05 and 2011-12 figures are NSSO Employment-Unemployment Survey rounds; the 2017-18 and 2023-24 figures are the Periodic Labour Force Survey, which replaced the EUS with a changed sampling design and stratification (P-02). The direction of both movements is not in doubt and the magnitude across the join is: a decline measured on one instrument and a rise measured on another do not subtract.
whatHappened: Rural female participation rose from 24.6% to 47.6%. But the self-employed share of employed women rose from 51.9% to 67.4%, their regular-salaried share fell to a seven-year low of 15.9%, rural women's wage-work share fell from 10.5% to 7.8%, and female self-employed monthly earnings fell even in nominal terms from ₹5,935 to ₹5,497. Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2023 characterises it as a distress-led increase in self-employment, with the self-employed share of women rising from 50% before COVID to 60% after.
caseFor: Nearly doubling female participation in six years is a genuine change in who is counted as working, and dismissing it as reclassification assumes the earlier low figures were correct when they were themselves criticised as undercounting women's work. Rural women entering household enterprises is how female employment began in most economies that later industrialised. The direction is unambiguous even if its quality is arguable.
caseAgainst: Participation rose while every measure of what those women earn or hold moved the other way — fewer in salaried work, lower earnings, more in unpaid household enterprise labour. That pattern is what distress entry looks like: households sending more members to work because income fell. And the ILO's modelled estimate for India is about 32% against PLFS's 41.7%, a nine-point gap that suggests definitional artefact rather than labour market change.
shockExposure: COVID is central and cuts both ways — it drove distress entry and also drove reverse migration into household enterprises. The pre-2020 rise from 23.3% to 30.0% predates it.

unmeasured.what: Whether the increase is paid market entry, reclassified unpaid work, or distress entry
unmeasured.why: No instrument separates the three. PLFS counts unpaid helpers as employed and asks no question that would distinguish them. Reclassified never-defined to not-collected on 2026-08-01: the quantity is defined and the denominator is defined; what is missing is collection on that base, not an agreed definition.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A time-use-linked labour module, or a PLFS supplement on paid versus unpaid activity within household enterprises

sources.name: Azim Premji University, State of Working India 2023

title: The four labour codes
summary: Twenty-nine central labour laws consolidated into four codes: the Code on Wages (2019) and the Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety codes (all September 2020), passed amid an opposition walkout and brought into force on 21 November 2025 after five years of deferral.
claimAtLaunch: Replace an ossified and widely evaded regime with a simplified framework that would extend social security, encourage formal hiring, and give employers the flexibility to grow.
whatHappened: The codes raise the threshold requiring government permission for retrenchment or closure from 100 to 300 workers, raise thresholds for standing orders, require 60 days' notice before a strike, expand fixed-term employment, and give gig and platform workers their first statutory recognition. Implementation was deferred year after year pending state rules; the codes took effect on 21 November 2025 and central rules were notified on 8 May 2026, with states at varying stages. The government claims social security coverage rose from 19% of the workforce in 2015 to 64% in 2025.
caseFor: The regime being replaced protected a small formal minority while pushing everyone else into informality — a firm crossing 100 workers faced permission requirements that gave it strong reason never to cross it. Raising the threshold to 300 removes a barrier to firms growing past the size where formal jobs appear. The codes also give gig and platform workers statutory standing for the first time, and mandate appointment letters and gratuity for fixed-term workers after one year.
caseAgainst: The 300-worker threshold means most Indian firms can now retrench or close without prior permission, which is a substantial transfer of power to employers presented as a growth measure. The 60-day strike notice constrains the only leverage workers hold. Fixed-term employment is legitimised rather than limited. And the codes passed during an opposition walkout, then sat unimplemented for five years — a reform whose urgency was asserted but not demonstrated by the pace of its own enactment.
revisitTrigger: The codes came into force in November 2025 and the formal-work share is measured annually with a lag, so this is not yet due rather than not gathered. Re-test on the PLFS written-contract and social-security shares for 2027 and 2028; if no post-implementation reading has appeared by then, it becomes an absence.
shockExposure: COVID intervened between passage and implementation and is the stated reason for much of the delay.
caveat: In force only since 21 November 2025 with central rules notified 8 May 2026. No outcome data exists. Any assessment before roughly 2028 is a judgement about the design, not about what it did.

sources.name: Ministry of Labour and Employment, PIB, 21 November 2025

title: Formalisation: registration against jobs
summary: The government cites 6.2 crore net EPFO subscriber additions between September 2017 and March 2024, and RBI KLEMS figures of 17.19 crore additional jobs over 2014-24 against 2.9 crore over 2004-14, as evidence of large-scale job creation.
whatHappened: EPFO net additions include members re-joining after a gap and members switching employers. One analysis of 4.86 crore net additions across FY2020 to FY2023 found roughly 2.27 crore genuinely new payroll entries and about 42 lakh of net formalisation. RBI KLEMS is a total factor productivity framework that takes employment as an input from PLFS and the national accounts, so citing its output as independent evidence of job creation is circular. The share of workers with a written contract or any social security remained around 11-12% throughout.
assessmentNote: Written 2026-08-05 (adversarial triage 3); this record previously carried a verdict with no stated reasoning. TWO CLAIMS WERE MADE FROM ONE SET OF NUMBERS AND THEY ARE MEASURED SEPARATELY HERE. Job creation: not supported. Net EPFO additions count re-joiners and employer-switchers, and the one decomposition retrieved turns 4.86 crore net additions into roughly 2.27 crore genuinely new payroll entries; KLEMS cannot corroborate it because KLEMS takes employment as an input from the same surveys, so the citation is circular. Formalisation: partly supported, and the split is the reason for the score. The count of workers inside the formal net did rise, and bringing provident fund and pension to a worker who had none is a real gain whether or not the job is new. But the DIRECT measure of formality - a written contract or any social security - stayed at about 11 to 12 per cent throughout, which is the outcome that would have shown formalisation happening rather than registration rising. Partly, therefore, on registration having risen while the two claims built on it do not follow. What is NOT measured is jobs created as distinct from registrations, entered below as an absence; no instrument retrieved separates them.
caseFor: Formalising an existing informal job is a real gain even when it is not a new job — it brings provident fund, pension and insurance to a worker who had none, and the count of workers inside the formal net genuinely rose. The e-Shram registration of over 30 crore unorganised workers created the first database capable of delivering benefits to people the state previously could not identify.
caseAgainst: The claims made from these numbers are not the claims the numbers support. Presenting net payroll additions as jobs created counts the same worker repeatedly as they change employers, and citing KLEMS as corroboration cites the survey back to itself. Meanwhile the direct measure of formality — written contract or social security — barely moved, which is the outcome that would have shown formalisation actually happening.
claimAtLaunch: That 6.2 crore net EPFO subscriber additions between September 2017 and March 2024, and RBI KLEMS figures of 17.19 crore additional jobs over 2014-24 against 2.9 crore over 2004-14, evidence large-scale job creation and formalisation.
shockExposure: COVID caused a large exit from and subsequent re-entry into formal payroll, inflating net additions in the recovery years.

unmeasured.what: Jobs created, as distinct from payroll registrations
unmeasured.why: India has no establishment-level new-hire register. EPFO counts subscribers, not first-time entrants; KLEMS estimates rather than measures. Reclassified never-defined to not-collected on 2026-08-01: the quantity is defined and the denominator is defined; what is missing is collection on that base, not an agreed definition.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A payroll-linked longitudinal new-hire register of the kind most comparable economies maintain

title: Educated youth unemployment
summary: Unemployment in India rises with education. The ILO and Institute for Human Development India Employment Report 2024 found youth were 82.9% of all unemployed, graduate unemployment stood at 29.1% against 3.4% for those who cannot read or write, and the secondary-plus-educated share of unemployed youth rose from 35.2% in 2000 to 65.7% in 2022.
whatHappened: Female graduates faced 34.5% unemployment against male graduates at 26.4%. The scale of competition for formal work is visible in government recruitment: 1.8 crore applicants for about 78,000 posts in FY2020-21, and 1.87 crore for about 38,000 in FY2021-22, against a total usual-status unemployed population PLFS puts at roughly 2.07 crore. Skill India and PMKVY trained about 1.6 crore people; the CAG's December 2025 performance audit found 41% of certified candidates placed, while a March 2023 parliamentary reply put placement since inception at 17.7%.
caseFor: Rising educated unemployment partly reflects success: far more young Indians now complete secondary and tertiary education than a decade ago, and an educated person can afford to wait for suitable work in a way an illiterate labourer cannot, so measured unemployment rises even as welfare improves. Youth unemployment did fall from 17.8% to 10.2% on PLFS, and skilling infrastructure was built where almost none existed.
caseAgainst: An economy where a graduate is nine times likelier to be unemployed than someone who cannot read is failing at the specific task of converting education into work. Two crore applicants for tens of thousands of posts is not queue behaviour, it is the absence of alternatives. And a flagship skilling programme placing between 18% and 41% of trainees, with the CAG finding 87% of batches lacking verifiable attendance records, did not build the bridge it was funded to build.
shockExposure: COVID disrupted hiring and examinations across 2020-2022, but the educated-unemployment pattern predates it and the ILO report's baseline runs from 2000.

unmeasured.what: Independently verified placement outcomes for skill-programme trainees
unmeasured.why: PMKVY placement figures are self-reported and administrative; the CAG found 87% of batches lacked verifiable biometric attendance and 94% of records lacked valid bank details. Reclassified not-published to not-collected on 2026-08-01: the placement figures are published; what is absent is independent verification, which was never performed. Nothing exists that could be produced under compulsion.
unmeasured.wouldFill: An EPFO-linked tracer study following trainees into payroll records, which the CAG recommended

sources.name: ILO and IHD, India Employment Report 2024

title: The 2020 migrant exodus and its missing record
summary: The March 2020 lockdown, announced with four hours' notice, triggered the largest internal migration in India's recent history as urban informal workers walked, cycled and rode home. The government's figure is about 1.04 crore returnees; independent estimates run to roughly 3 crore.
whatHappened: Between 1 May and 31 August 2020, 4,611 Shramik Special trains carried about 63 lakh workers. The Labour Ministry told Parliament that no data was maintained on deaths during the exodus or on job losses, and that the question of compensation therefore did not arise. The Railways Minister separately told the Rajya Sabha that 97 people died aboard Shramik Special trains to 9 September 2020, and an RTI response indicated the government held data it had declined to give Parliament. Independent tallies recorded about 198 road-accident deaths to 2 June 2020 and about 971 non-COVID lockdown-related deaths to July 2020. The e-Shram portal, launched August 2021, has since registered over 30.98 crore unorganised workers.
caseFor: A national lockdown decided in days could not have been sequenced perfectly, and the Shramik trains moved 63 lakh people in four months once the scale became clear. e-Shram exists because the crisis exposed that the state could not identify its own informal workforce, and 30 crore registrations is a genuine remedy to that.
caseAgainst: Four hours' notice for a country where most workers are paid daily and live where they work was a choice, and its consequence was foreseeable. That no count of deaths was maintained — while the Railways held data it did not surrender to Parliament — means the human cost of the largest internal displacement in decades has no official record and now cannot be constructed. A state that could not say how many died also could not compensate anyone, which was the stated reason it did not.
differentFactsNote: The government's case rests on the evacuation - 63 lakh moved on Shramik trains - and on e-Shram, built because the crisis exposed that the state could not identify its own informal workforce. The critics' case rests on the four hours' notice and on the absence of any mortality record. The second is not a quantity but the stated absence of one, and this record holds that it can no longer be constructed, so no ledger can carry both.
shockExposure: This record is the shock. Its confound runs the other way: it distorts every employment series for 2020-21 and 2021-22.

unmeasured.what: The number of workers who returned home during the 2020 exodus
unmeasured.why: No official count was attempted. The government figure of about 1.04 crore and independent estimates near 3 crore differ by a factor of three with no reconciliation.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A national migration survey, or the Census, which has not been conducted since 2011

unmeasured.why: The Labour Ministry told Parliament that no such data is maintained, and therefore that the question of compensation did not arise. That stated reason is contradicted: the Railways Minister told the Rajya Sabha that 97 people died aboard Shramik Special trains, and an RTI response indicated the government held data it had declined to give Parliament. So the absence is asserted as not-collected while evidence indicates at least partial withholding. Independent tallies reached about 971 lockdown-related non-COVID deaths.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A compiled audit of Railways, state and health ministry mortality records, some of which demonstrably exist

title: Structural transformation reversal
summary: India's employment structure moved backwards relative to its peers. Agriculture's employment share fell only 45.3% to 42.4% on ILO estimates and rose on PLFS after 2018-19, while industry's share stayed flat near 25%. Over the same decade Vietnam moved from 46.3% to 25.9% agricultural and 21.4% to 34.3% industrial employment.
whatHappened: India's vulnerable employment share — own-account and contributing family workers — remained the highest in the peer panel at about 72%. Employment elasticity of growth stayed low, and India adds roughly 2 million net jobs a year against a youth cohort entering at 7-8 million annually. This is the employment face of phase 2's finding that manufacturing's GDP share fell from 15.07% to 13.14% while Bangladesh's and Vietnam's rose.
caseFor: India's services-led path is genuinely different from the East Asian manufacturing model and has produced world-competitive sectors in IT, business services and pharmaceuticals that employ millions at high productivity. Global conditions after 2014 were far less favourable to export manufacturing than during Vietnam's or China's take-off, and automation has weakened the labour absorption that manufacturing once offered anywhere.
caseAgainst: The peer panel disposes of the global-conditions defence: Vietnam and Bangladesh transformed their employment structures over exactly the same decade under the same world economy. Services at India's productivity frontier employ a small fraction of the workforce and cannot absorb 7-8 million annual entrants. An economy whose agricultural employment share is rising while its demographic dividend window is open is not choosing a different path to the same place.
shockExposure: COVID accelerated the agricultural reabsorption, but the divergence from peers is a decade-long trend that predates it.
